text: Last lesson injected a backend as a parameter. This lesson formalizes what kind of object that parameter should be: a shared interface that a simulator, a noisy simulator, and real hardware all implement identically, so algorithm code never needs to know or care which one it's talking to.

This lesson covers defining an abstract backend interface using Python's abc.ABC, implementing that interface for a local simulator and a real-hardware backend, why this makes CI testing, local development, and production runs use the exact same algorithm code, how to swap backends via configuration, and the specific place this pattern breaks down.

An abstract base class defines the contract every backend must fulfill. Here, QuantumBackend requires a run method — given a circuit and a shot count, return a dictionary of bitstring to count — and a name method for logging and reproducibility records. Both a local simulator class and a real IBM hardware class implement this identical contract underneath, each in their own way.

With both implementations satisfying the same interface, algorithm code written against the interface works unmodified against either. run_bell_experiment takes a backend parameter and never imports a concrete simulator or hardware class directly. Calling it with a local simulator backend works for CI and local development; calling it with a real IBM hardware backend, with zero changes to the function itself, is what runs in production. This is the direct payoff of last lesson's separation — swapping the backend is a one-line change at the call site, not a code change inside the algorithm.

Not every backend capability belongs in the shared interface, and forcing one in is a common over-engineering mistake. Real hardware exposes things a simulator fundamentally cannot — queue position, calibration data, qubit-specific error rates. Adding a method like get_calibration_data to the shared interface just because real hardware has it is capability leakage; a simulator would have to fake a meaningless return value. Instead, expose hardware-specific capabilities through a separate, optional interface that algorithm code only reaches for when it explicitly knows it's targeting real hardware.

Next lesson tackles a harder version of this same problem: designing for multiple SDKs at once, specifically Qiskit and Microsoft's Q-sharp, which can't simply share a Python process the way two Qiskit-based backends can.
